questions.question: List: 1→2→3→4→NULL. Given pointer p to node 2: q=p->next; p->next=q->next; free(q);  What does the list look like after?
questions.solutionApproach: q points to node 3. p->next=q->next means node 2's next now points to node 4 (skipping 3). Free q (node 3). Result: 1→2→4→NULL.

questions.question: You're given a pointer to a node X in a singly linked list, and told X is NOT the last node. What's the worst-case time to delete X using only this pointer?
questions.solutionApproach: Since X is not last, use the copy-trick: copy X->next's data into X, then delete X->next (which requires only updating X->next = X->next->next). O(1).
questions.answer: O(1) — the copy-next-and-delete-next trick works since X is guaranteed not to be the last node.

questions.question: Why is binary search NOT efficient on a sorted singly linked list, even though the list is sorted?
questions.solutionApproach: Binary search needs O(1) random access to the middle element at each step. A linked list requires O(n) traversal just to REACH the middle, destroying the log n advantage — overall becomes O(n) instead of O(log n).
questions.answer: No random access — reaching the 'middle' element itself takes O(n) traversal, so binary search degrades to O(n) overall.

questions.question: For a circular singly-linked-list-based queue, why is pointing the single external pointer to the FRONT node a bad design choice?
questions.solutionApproach: With pointer at front, front access is O(1), but enqueue (which must reach rear to insert after it) requires traversing the ENTIRE list from front to rear = O(n). Pointing at rear instead gives O(1) for BOTH (front = rear->next).
questions.answer: Enqueue would need O(n) traversal to reach rear from front — pointing at REAR instead gives O(1) access to both ends.
